processing: Tea bushes are covered with black shade for about 20 days before picking, which raises amino acids and lowers catechins. The leaf is then made as gyokuro, steamed and rolled into fine needles as is usual for the type; the top grade is hand-picked.
harvest_season: Spring, after about 20 days of shading. Hand-picked lots are the prized ones.
appearance_dry: Typical of gyokuro: fine, deep green needles with a soft sheen.
appearance_liquor: Typically a pale, clear yellow-green, and thick in the mouth for a small pour.
appearance_wet: Soft, tender, bright green leaves, as is usual for a shaded tea.
taste_profile: Strong umami with little bitterness, a clear sweetness and a rich aroma; the second cup moves closer to a regular sencha.

brewing.notes: Use water at about 40 to 45 C, barely warm to the touch, and let the very last drops fall into the cup; that is where the flavour concentrates. Raise the heat a little for later steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest, usually within the current year, as with other gyokuro. Grade matters more than year here: hand-picked lots and the named teas of local gyokuro masters sit at the top. It does not age, so keep it sealed and cold.
description:
Asahina gyokuro comes from the Asahina river valley in Okabe, now part of Fujieda in Shizuoka. Along with Uji and Yame, the area is counted among Japan's three big gyokuro regions, which is striking in a prefecture better known for everyday sencha.

The bushes spend about 20 days under black shade before picking. Less sun means more amino acids and fewer catechins, and that is the whole point: a cup that tastes savoury and sweet rather than brisk.

Drunk properly, it is a small, intense thing. Very cool water, about 40 to 45 C, gives strong umami and very little bitterness, and the second cup already drinks more like a sencha. The usual mistake is hot water, which throws away what you paid for.

Look for the words Asahina tezumi hon-gyokuro for the hand-picked style. The area also has eight growers known as gyokuro masters whose teas carry their own names. The local roadside station, Gyokuro no Sato, is the easy place to taste it in a tea room.

At the end, try the spent leaves with a little soy sauce, as is common with gyokuro.
history:
Little is documented in accessible form about when gyokuro growing began at Asahina or who started it. What can be said is that the name is firmly established: Asahina appears among the named teas of Shizuoka under the Okabe area, and today it is presented as one of the three main gyokuro regions of Japan.

The recent story is about visitors. A roadside station with a tea room, Gyokuro no Sato, serves the tea.
